title: Kabir (the dohas, one a day for a week)
hook: Kabir (the dohas, one a day for a week)
carry: the musk is in the deer
tomorrow: Tulsidas (the Ramcharitmanas opening and the Hanuman Chalisa, verse by verse)

segments.voice: Yesterday: Kabir's second doha. No one became wise from books alone; whoever reads the two and a half letters of love becomes the pandit.

A deer moves through the forest, head low, nose working. There's a scent in the air, rich and sweet, and it's maddening, because it's everywhere and nowhere. The deer checks behind a tree. Under a bush. Down by the stream. The scent is just as strong in each place, and never any closer. It keeps searching until it's worn out. Kabir put this deer in two lines. It's the third doha this week, and the last day with the weaver of Kashi.
screen: `A SCENT IN THE FOREST.` → `EVERYWHERE AND NOWHERE.` → `THE DEER KEEPS SEARCHING.`

segments.voice: The doha begins, in Hindi, kasturi kundal basai. Kasturi is musk, the prized scent. Roughly: the musk lives in the deer's own navel, and the deer goes searching for it through the forest. Then the second line: just so, Ram is in every body, every heart, and the world doesn't see. The joke is gentle, and the deer stands for anyone who searches. Every place smelled of musk because the deer brought it to every place. Ram, in Kabir's mouth, is the name his teacher cried out on the steps at Kashi. But Kabir's Ram isn't held in one temple or one image. In this doha, Ram is in every heart, and the trouble is only that people look everywhere else first. Put the three dohas together. Go looking for the bad one, and you end up searching your own heart. Read book after book, and the lesson is still two and a half letters, love. Search the whole forest for God, and the scent was in you all along. Three hunts, each turning back toward the hunter. Kabir's life ends, tradition says, with one more turn. When he died, his followers, Hindus and Muslims, each wanted to give him their own last rites. Some say they argued over the body. When they lifted the sheet, there was no body at all, only a heap of flowers. So each group took half the flowers, and honored him in its own way.
screen: `THE MUSK IS IN THE DEER.` · `RAM IN EVERY HEART.` · `THREE HUNTS, TURNED BACK.` · then, large: `ONLY FLOWERS UNDER THE SHEET.`

segments.voice: Let the searching part of you rest, and notice the breath coming in and going out without going anywhere to get it. If your mind runs off into the forest, after a plan or a worry, notice it the way you'd notice the deer, and come back to what's already here. If you pray, you can rest in God as near as your own breath.
Kabir. The weaver-poet of Kashi. Today's doha: the musk is in the deer's own navel, and it searches the forest; Ram is in every heart, and the world doesn't see.
Your line: the musk is in the deer. The scent was coming from the one who searched. That's day nine hundred twenty-three.

screen: `DAY 923 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: TULSIDAS (THE RAMCHARITMANAS OPENING AND THE HANUMAN CHALISA, VERSE BY VERSE).`

howItsDone: The musk deer doha is quoted as a saying about looking for God far away, and the story of the flowers under Kabir's sheet is told by people of more than one community who honor him.

chat.says: In Kabir's musk deer poem, why does the deer never find the smell?
options: The musk is in its own navel; Kabir says Ram is in every heart like that.
The musk is hidden too deep in the forest for any deer to reach it.
The deer gives up searching too soon and goes home without it.
chat.meaning: The scent was coming from the deer itself. Just so, the doha says, Ram is in every heart, and the world doesn't see.

Ram.meaning: a name of God; for Kabir, the one in every heart

doha.meaning: a couplet: two rhyming lines, easy to remember
